T1: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they reduce labor cost and increase convenience for small‑garden tasks. Who benefits: Homeowners with small gardens who need a versatile tool for multiple chores.. Why behaviour changes: The demand for garden tractors is driven by the desire to save time and money on tasks like mowing, weeding, and clearing debris, which are traditionally done by hand or with expensive hired labor.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling tractors at a premium price, offering attachments, and building a dealer network that provides service and parts, creating recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Small‑garden homeowners are willing to invest in a machine that can perform multiple tasks.; The cost of owning and operating a tractor is lower than the cost of hiring professional services for small‑garden work.; Deere can produce tractors at scale and distribute them through its existing dealer network.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor, sales will be driven by homeowners who purchase it for multiple‑task use.; Deere’s dealer network will be able to sell and service the tractors, generating additional revenue from parts and accessories..

T2: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they represent a status symbol and a symbol of modern living, increasing social prestige and community acceptance. Who benefits: Homeowners who seek to demonstrate affluence and modern lifestyle through ownership of a new consumer product.. Why behaviour changes: The demand for garden tractors is driven by the desire to keep up with neighbors and peers who already own them, and by the broader cultural shift in the 1960s toward consumerism and aspirational products.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by positioning tractors as premium lifestyle items, offering limited editions or custom designs, and leveraging its brand reputation to command higher prices.. Assumptions: Homeowners in suburban communities are influenced by peer norms and desire to signal status.; The tractor is perceived as a modern, aspirational product rather than a purely functional tool.; Deere can market the tractor as a lifestyle product through advertising and dealer promotions.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor with distinctive styling, sales will be driven by homeowners who purchase it as a status symbol.; Deere’s dealer network will be able to upsell accessories and services, creating additional revenue from lifestyle‑oriented purchases..

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two tractor concepts: a functional, low‑cost model (e.g., basic lawn and garden tractor) and a lifestyle‑oriented model (e.g., limited‑edition, custom design, premium price). They indicate which they would buy and the price they would pay. The survey also asks about willingness to pay for a status‑symbol feature.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region. Stratify by household income to reflect small‑garden homeowners.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants choosing the functional model versus the lifestyle model. Secondary: average price willingness for each model.. Predictions: T1: Functional model will be chosen by at least 60% of participants, and average willingness to pay for it will be below $1,500.; T2: Lifestyle model will be chosen by at least 60% of participants, and average willingness to pay for it will be above $2,000.. Decision rule: If functional model ≥ 60% and lifestyle model ≤ 40% → T1 is supported. If lifestyle model ≥ 60% and functional model ≤ 40% → T2 is supported. If neither meets threshold → insufficient evidence to justify investment.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑holder farming and home‑garden use, leveraging existing dealer network and tractor engineering. Conduct a limited pilot test (e.g., 50 units) to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand for lawn and garden tractors. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑holder farming and home‑garden use, leveraging existing dealer network and tractor engineering. Conduct a limited pilot test (e.g., 50 units) to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners with small gardens who need a versatile tool for multiple chores, and small‑holder farmers who require a compact, affordable tractor for light tasks.. Value proposition: A consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor that reduces labor cost and increases convenience for small‑garden tasks, sold through Deere’s dealer network with attachments and service.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed consumer preference survey (X1) to measure willingness to pay for a functional model versus a lifestyle model, and use the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a pilot.. Uncertainty: The exact size of the consumer market for lawn and garden tractors in 1962 is unknown; the willingness to pay for a premium lifestyle model is also uncertain. The pilot test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the survey shows the functional model chosen by <40% of participants and average willingness to pay below $1,500, the evidence would contradict T1 and support a no‑expansion recommendation.; If the survey shows the lifestyle model chosen by <40% and average willingness to pay below $2,000, the evidence would contradict T2 and also support a no‑expansion recommendation.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon because it offers a reliable, automatic distress signal that can be used in remote areas where other communication methods fail. Who benefits: Hikers, campers, and other outdoor adventurers who need a safety device that can be activated without manual intervention.. Why behaviour changes: In a life-threatening situation, these users will prioritize a device that can automatically send a distress signal to SAR responders, reducing the need for manual signaling and increasing survival chances.. How value is captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers through retail channels or online, capturing the full retail price while leveraging its existing marine survival light distribution network.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in 2002 was large enough to justify a consumer product.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides automatic distress signaling.; Regulatory requirements (e.g., mandatory registration) support consumer adoption.. Predictions: If offered at a price comparable to survival lights, at least 10% of surveyed outdoor recreationists would indicate intent to purchase within 12 months.; Sales would be concentrated in regions with high outdoor recreation participation (e.g., national parks, mountain ranges)..

T2: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a 406 MHz distress beacon because it offers a lightweight, automatic distress signal that can be integrated into existing outdoor gear, reducing the need for separate devices. Who benefits: Hikers, campers, and other outdoor adventurers who already carry survival kits and want a single device that can send a distress signal without manual activation.. Why behaviour changes: In a remote emergency, users will prefer a device that can be activated automatically and that seamlessly integrates with their existing gear, eliminating the need to carry multiple items.. How value is captured: ACR can sell the beacon as a plug-and-play add-on to existing outdoor gear (e.g., backpacks, tents) through outdoor retailers and online marketplaces, capturing a premium for integration.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in 2002 was large enough to justify a consumer product.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that integrates with existing gear.; Regulatory requirements support integration without compromising functionality.. Predictions: If offered as a plug-and-play add-on at a price comparable to survival lights, at least 8% of surveyed outdoor recreationists would indicate intent to purchase within 12 months.; Sales would be concentrated among users who already carry survival kits and value integration..

Test "Consumer Intent Test for Outdoor Recreation Distress Beacon" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants are recruited via outdoor recreation forums and outdoor retailer newsletters. They are shown a product description for a 406 MHz distress beacon (either automatic distress signal or plug-and-play integration). They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for outdoor recreation use?" (yes/no). For T1, the product description emphasizes automatic distress signal in remote areas. For T2, it emphasizes integration with existing outdoor gear. Both. Sample: 200 participants, split evenly between two groups (100 per group). Each group receives the product description corresponding to one theory.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who indicate "yes" when asked if they would buy).. Predictions: T1: Group receiving the automatic distress signal description will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than group receiving the integration description.; T2: Group receiving the integration description will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than group receiving the automatic distress signal description.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent rates between the two groups is at least 10 percentage points, the theory that predicts the larger difference is supported. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, the evidence is inconclusive.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a consumer-focused 406 MHz distress beacon for outdoor recreation, targeting hikers and campers. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., 5,000 units) through outdoor retailers and online channels, and use the existing distribution network to reach individual buyers. Conduct a low-cost survey test (as proposed) to validate purchase intent before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a consumer-focused 406 MHz distress beacon for outdoor recreation, targeting hikers and campers. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., 5,000 units) through outdoor retailers and online channels, using the existing distribution network to reach individual buyers. Conduct a low-cost survey test (as proposed) to validate purchase intent before scaling. Target customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, campers) who need a reliable automatic distress signal for remote areas.. Value proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that automatically sends a distress signal in remote environments, providing peace of mind and potentially saving lives.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed consumer intent test (X1) to measure purchase intent for automatic distress signal versus plug-and-play integration. If the test shows a ≥10 percentage point difference in favor of automatic distress signal, proceed to full. Uncertainty: Consumer demand for a 406 MHz distress beacon is uncertain; the test is needed to validate purchase intent. Regulatory requirements (e.g., registration) are known to exist but may not fully drive adoption.. Would change if: If the test shows a ≥10 percentage point difference in favor of plug-and-play integration, shift focus to that proposition.; If the test shows purchase intent below 5% for both propositions, conclude that consumer demand is insufficient and recommend no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Homeowners with small gardens who need a versatile tool for multiple chores.. Why behaviour changes: The demand for garden tractors is driven by the desire to save time and money on tasks like mowing, weeding, and clearing debris, which are traditionally done by hand or with expensive hired labor.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling tractors at a premium price, offering attachments, and building a dealer network that provides service and parts, creating recurring revenue.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor, sales will be driven by homeowners who purchase it for multiple‑task use.; Deere’s dealer network will be able to sell and service the tractors, generating additional revenue from parts and accessories..

Test "Consumer Survey on Purchase Motivation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized presentation of two product descriptions. Participants are homeowners with small gardens who have not purchased a lawn and garden tractor. They are shown a description of a basic, functional tractor (cost, features, maintenance) and a description of the same tractor positioned as a status symbol (limited edition, custom design, prestige). They are asked which description they would choose and why. The survey also asks about willingness to pay a premium for the status‑oriented version.. Sample: 200 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region. Randomly assigned to view either functional or status description.. Measure: Proportion of participants choosing the status‑oriented description and their stated willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 20% above functional price).. Predictions: T1: Most participants will choose the functional description and show low willingness to pay a premium, indicating that cost‑of‑ownership and convenience drive purchase.; T2: Most participants will choose the status‑oriented description and show willingness to pay a premium, indicating that prestige and peer influence drive purchase.. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing the status description is at least 15 percentage points higher than the functional description, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing status and lifestyle. If the functional description is at least 15 percentage points higher, focus on. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they reduce labor cost and increase convenience for small‑garden tasks. Who benefits: Homeowners with small gardens who need a versatile tool for multiple chores.. Why behaviour changes: The demand for garden tractors is driven by the desire to save time and money on tasks like mowing, weeding, and clearing debris, which are traditionally done by hand or with expensive hired labor.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling tractors at a premium price, offering attachments, and building a dealer network that provides service and parts, creating recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Small‑garden homeowners are willing to invest in a machine that can perform multiple tasks.; The cost of owning and operating a tractor is lower than the cost of hiring professional services for small‑garden work.; Deere can produce tractors at scale and distribute them through its existing dealer network.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor, sales will be driven by homeowners who purchase it for multiple‑task use.; Deere’s dealer network will be able to sell and service the tractors, generating additional revenue from parts and accessories..

T2: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they represent a status symbol and a symbol of modern living, increasing social prestige and community acceptance. Who benefits: Homeowners who seek to demonstrate affluence and modern lifestyle through ownership of a new consumer product.. Why behaviour changes: The demand for garden tractors is driven by the desire to keep up with neighbors and peers who already own them, and by the broader cultural shift in the 1960s toward consumerism and aspirational products.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by positioning tractors as premium lifestyle items, offering limited editions or custom designs, and leveraging its brand reputation to command higher prices.. Assumptions: Homeowners in suburban communities are influenced by peer norms and desire to signal status.; The tractor is perceived as a modern, aspirational product rather than a purely functional tool.; Deere can market the tractor as a lifestyle product through advertising and dealer promotions..
